subject: Computer Networking
title: Cookies and Sessions
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Cookies and Sessions.

hook.text: You log into a site, browse ten pages, and stay logged in. HTTP is stateless — so how does the site know you?

buildup.text: After you log in, the server sends a small token called a cookie. Your browser sends it with every request.

discovery.text: The cookie contains a session ID. The server matches it to your account and remembers who you are.

twist.text: Tracking cookies follow you across sites for ads. That's why browsers now block third-party cookies.

climax.text: Without cookies, you'd re-enter your password on every single page. The web would be unusable.

punchline.text: Cookies give the stateless web a memory.

quiz.question: Why are cookies necessary for web sessions?
options: HTTP is stateless, so cookies carry identity between requests
Servers can't store any data without cookies

details.summary: Cookies are small data fragments servers store in your browser to remember you across HTTP requests. Session cookies expire when you close the browser; persistent cookies last longer. Sessions use cookies to maintain login state, shopping carts, and preferences across stateless HTTP.
details.whyItMatters: Cookies make the stateless web feel stateful. Without them, you would need to log in on every page load and your shopping cart would empty with each click.
takeaways: Cookies store small data in the browser for state tracking
Session cookies expire on browser close; persistent ones last longer
Sessions track login state and user data across requests

faq.question: Why are cookies a privacy concern?
faq.answer: Third-party cookies track your browsing across different websites, building advertising profiles. Companies use cookies to follow you around the web. Browser makers are phasing out third-party cookies. First-party cookies from the site you visit are generally necessary for functionality.

faq.question: How do sessions work with cookies?
faq.answer: The server creates a unique session ID when you log in and sends it as a cookie. Your browser sends this cookie with every request. The server looks up your session data using the ID to identify you. When you log out, the server destroys the session.
